notes.meaning: God told Moses that one final plague would strike Pharaoh and the land of Egypt. After this terrible blow, the king would not simply permit the Israelites to go, but would urgently drive them out with no conditions attached. God had promised full deliverance from the beginning, and that promise was now about to come true.

The Lord instructed the Israelite men and women to ask their Egyptian neighbors for valuable goods of silver and gold. This was not borrowing under false pretenses or stealing, but collecting back wages for generations of unpaid forced labor. God made sure His people would not leave their long slavery empty-handed.

The Lord worked in the minds of the Egyptians so they gladly gave the Israelites whatever was requested. Even Pharaoh's royal officials held Moses in deep respect and awe because of the great wonders God had performed through him. God has the power to change the hearts of former oppressors to show favor to His people.

Moses delivered God's warning directly to Pharaoh before walking away from the royal palace. The Lord declared that at midnight He would pass throughout Egypt to execute judgment. Unlike the earlier plagues that were brought about through signs from a staff, God Himself was coming to strike the blow.

Every firstborn male throughout Egypt was condemned to die, from Pharaoh's royal heir down to the child of the poorest slave girl grinding grain. Even the firstborn among the cattle would perish, striking down animals that the Egyptians treated as gods. This showed that no rank or false god could shield anyone from God's righteous judgment.

A terrible wailing would rise up across the whole land of Egypt. The grief would be greater than anything Egypt had ever experienced before or would ever experience again. The nation that had caused God's people to groan in bitter sorrow was now brought to weep over its own loss.

Among the Israelites, complete stillness and safety would prevail, so that not even a watchdog would bark at any person or animal. This phrase was a common saying meaning that God's people would enjoy perfect peace and no harm. The sharp contrast showed everyone that the Lord makes a clear separation between His people and the world.

Moses declared that Pharaoh's top leaders would come bowing down to him, pleading for Israel to take everyone and leave. After finishing this solemn message, Moses walked out of Pharaoh's presence in great anger. His anger was not selfish, but a holy indignation at Pharaoh's stubborn rebellion against God.

The Lord reminded Moses that Pharaoh would stubbornly refuse to listen. This refusal did not catch God off guard, but served to display God's miraculous power in even greater ways before the eyes of the world. God remains completely in control even when wicked rulers refuse His commands.

Moses and Aaron had performed all nine plagues before Pharaoh, yet the king's heart was hardened and he still refused to let the people go. This statement wraps up the story of the first nine wonders before the final Passover judgment begins. Repeatedly ignoring God's truth leaves a person stubbornly fixed in their own rebellion.

differ.view: Reformed Christians teach that God sovereignly decreed the hardening of Pharaoh's heart to display His absolute authority and judgment over a sinful ruler.
Methodists emphasize that Pharaoh freely hardened his own heart against God's merciful warnings first, and God gave him over to the natural consequence of his persistent choices.
